clinicalPearls: A disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium avium complex, ubiquitous environmental organisms found in soil and water, acquired through inhalation or ingestion
Disseminated disease occurs almost exclusively in profoundly immunocompromised hosts, classically people with advanced HIV and very low CD4 counts
The typical presentation is insidious fever, night sweats, weight loss and wasting, fatigue, and abdominal symptoms with hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy
Cytopenias (especially anaemia) and a raised alkaline phosphatase are common laboratory clues in advanced HIV
Diagnosis is best confirmed by mycobacterial blood cultures, with bone marrow, lymph node, or liver biopsy showing acid-fast bacilli and granulomas as alternatives

Treatment is prolonged combination antimycobacterial therapy (a macrolide-based regimen) together with antiretroviral therapy for immune restoration, and macrolide monotherapy must be avoided to prevent resistance
Starting antiretroviral therapy can precipitate an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome with paradoxical worsening, particularly focal lymphadenitis
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium avium complex organisms are environmental mycobacteria encountered through water and soil, entering the body via the gastrointestinal or respiratory tract. In people with intact cell-mediated immunity infection is contained, but in those with profound immunosuppression, particularly advanced HIV with very low CD4 counts, the organisms proliferate within macrophages and disseminate widely through the reticuloendothelial system. Heavy infiltration of bone marrow, liver, spleen, gut, and lymph nodes with mycobacteria-laden macrophages produces the constitutional wasting, cytopenias, organomegaly, and cholestatic liver findings that characterise disseminated disease.
additionalDifferentials: Disseminated fungal infection such as histoplasmosis or talaromycosis
Other opportunistic infections causing fever and wasting in advanced HIV
Drug reaction or antiretroviral-related immune reconstitution syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Mycobacterial blood cultures for Mycobacterium avium complex
Bone marrow, lymph node, or liver biopsy with acid-fast staining and mycobacterial culture
CD4 count and HIV viral load to assess immune status
Full blood count for cytopenias and liver function tests including alkaline phosphatase
Cross-sectional imaging for hepatosplenomegaly and abdominal lymphadenopathy
Species identification and drug-susceptibility testing to distinguish from tuberculosis and guide therapy
redFlags: Progressive wasting with high fevers in a patient with very low CD4 count
Marked hepatosplenomegaly or bulky abdominal lymphadenopathy
Paradoxical worsening after starting antiretroviral therapy suggesting immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome
Features overlapping with disseminated tuberculosis requiring urgent differentiation
reference.prognosis: With combination antimycobacterial therapy and immune restoration through antiretroviral treatment, disseminated MAC is generally controllable and prognosis has improved markedly, though outcomes remain worse with very advanced immunosuppression or delayed diagnosis.
pitfalls: Using macrolide monotherapy, which rapidly selects for resistance
Failing to distinguish disseminated MAC from tuberculosis before committing to therapy
Overlooking the diagnosis in a wasting, febrile patient with advanced HIV
Not anticipating immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome when antiretroviral therapy is started
Discontinuing therapy prematurely before adequate immune recovery is achieved
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
IDSA/ATS guidelines on the management of non-tuberculous mycobacterial infections
management: Prolonged macrolide-based combination therapy is the mainstay, pairing a macrolide (azithromycin or clarithromycin) with ethambutol and often rifabutin, never as macrolide monotherapy
Start or optimise antiretroviral therapy to restore CD4-driven immunity in HIV
Anticipate and manage immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after antiretroviral therapy is begun
Provide supportive care for wasting, anaemia, and cholestasis
Continue antimycobacterial therapy until sustained immune recovery and clinical and microbiological response
Perform species identification and drug-susceptibility testing to distinguish from tuberculosis and guide the regimen
Maintain infectious diseases follow-up with adherence support
